Final i before the unlike vowel a becomes y.

samasa.vigraha: शतं वर्षाणि शतवर्षम्; शतवर्षं भवा शतवार्षिकी, तस्याम्
samasa.type: dvigu (समाहार) as the base of a taddhita
samasa.sense: a drought that lasts a century

samasa.vigraha: न विद्यते अम्भः यस्यां सा अनम्भाः, तस्याम्
samasa.alt: It may also stand on its own as ‘when (the earth) is waterless’, with भुवि or जगति understood; the sense does not change.

samasa.vigraha: न योनिजा अयोनिजा; योनौ जायते इति योनिजा
samasa.type: nañ tatpuruṣa, its second member an upapada tatpuruṣa (योनिज)

morph.note: Future of सम् + √भू (भो + इष्य → भविष्य): ‘I shall come into being’. The prefix सम् gives the sense of appearing or being born.
Past participle of सम् + √स्तु: ‘praised’. The sages’ praise comes before her appearance: they call, and she appears.

mantras.anvaya: भूयः च शतवार्षिक्याम् अनम्भसि अनावृष्ट्यां (सत्यां) मुनिभिः संस्तुता (अहम्) अयोनिजा भूमौ सम्भविष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The locatives give the occasion (a waterless hundred-year drought); मुनिभिः संस्तुता gives the cause; the main clause is (अहम्) अयोनिजा भूमौ सम्भविष्यामि.
mantras.lit: And again, in a drought lasting a hundred years, without water, praised by the sages, I shall come into being on the earth, not born from a womb.
mantras.tr: And once more, when the earth lies a hundred years without rain or water, I shall appear on earth at the sages’ praise, born of no womb.
mantras.tr_note: ‘At the sages’ praise’ renders मुनिभिः संस्तुता (‘praised by the sages’) as the occasion of her coming.

comm.t: The third descent begins: a drought of a hundred years, the sages praise her, and she appears on earth अयोनिजा, born of no mother. Unlike the daughter of Yaśodā (11.42), this form has no human birth.

Verses 11.46–50 are one episode with three names: Śatākṣī (11.47), Śākambharī (11.49) and Durgā (11.50), all of the same appearance (तत्रैव, ‘right there’, 11.49). The tradition treats them as one Goddess named by three of her deeds.

indeclinable (adverb, correlative of यत्)

sandhi.note: Final t (voiced to d at word end, 8.2.39) becomes the nasal n before the m of मुनीन्.

sandhi.type: no change (final m before a vowel)
sandhi.rule: मोऽनुस्वारः (8.3.23) does not apply before a vowel
sandhi.note: The m is written with the i of इति. Inside the compound, शत + अक्षी → शताक्षी (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः, 6.1.101).
Before a sibilant the visarga may stand; the text keeps it here and in ततः शतेन.

samasa.vigraha: शतम् अक्षीणि यस्याः सा शताक्षी, ताम्
samasa.literal: she who has a hundred eyes
samasa.sense: Śatākṣī, the Hundred-eyed. At the end of a bahuvrīhi अक्षि takes the stem अक्ष (a samāsānta suffix), and the feminine is formed in -ī.

morph.note: Future of निर् + √ईक्ष् with iṭ (ईक्ष् + इष्य). √ईक्ष् is ātmanepadin, so the classical form would be निरीक्षिष्ये; the parasmaipada ending is an epic and Purāṇic licence (ārṣa).
The neuter relative used as a conjunction, ‘since, because’, answered by ततः ‘therefore’ at the end of the verse: यत् … ततः.
Future of the curādi stem कीर्तय- (कीर्तय + इष्य + अन्ति); with माम् … शताक्षीम् इति, ‘they will proclaim me as Śatākṣī’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः यत् (अहं) नेत्राणां शतेन मुनीन् निरीक्षिष्यामि, ततः मनुजाः मां शताक्षीम् इति कीर्तयिष्यन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: A causal clause (यत् … निरीक्षिष्यामि) and its correlative main clause (ततः … कीर्तयिष्यन्ति); इति marks the name.
mantras.lit: Then, since I shall look upon the sages with a hundred eyes, men will therefore proclaim me as ‘Śatākṣī’.
mantras.tr: Because I shall look upon the sages with a hundred eyes, men will call me Śatākṣī, the Hundred-eyed.
mantras.tr_note: The first ततः (‘then’) is left untranslated in tr; ‘the Hundred-eyed’ glosses the name.

comm.t: The first name of the third descent: she looks upon the sages with a hundred eyes, and so is called Śatākṣī. The text gives only the gaze; it does not say what the eyes do.

Later Śākta retellings fill the gap. In the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa the Hundred-eyed Goddess, seeing the suffering of the drought, weeps from all her eyes, and her tears become the rain that refills the rivers. The Devī Māhātmya itself says only that she looked.
A modern reading: the first thing the Goddess does in the famine is to see. Attention comes before relief.

flags.uncertain: यत्: read as the conjunction ‘since’, answered by ततः. It could also be taken as ‘when’ (‘when I look upon the sages …’); the sense is nearly the same.

sandhi.note: -aḥ before a becomes -o, and the following a is absorbed (avagraha). The m of अहम् is written with अखिलम्.

sandhi.type: no change (final m before a vowel)
sandhi.rule: मोऽनुस्वारः (8.3.23) does not apply before a vowel
sandhi.note: The m is written with the ā of आत्म-.
After a vowel other than a/ā, the visarga (as ru) appears as r before a vowel: शाकै + र् + आ. आ and वृष्टेः are simply written together.

samasa.vigraha: आत्मनः देहः आत्मदेहः; आत्मदेहात् समुद्भवः येषां ते, तैः
samasa.literal: whose origin is from one’s own body
samasa.alt: Also read as a pañcamī tatpuruṣa, आत्मदेहात् समुद्भवाः ‘arisen from my body’; the sense is the same.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (object genitive with an agent noun in -aka)

morph.note: Future of √भृ: roots in ṛ take the connecting vowel i in the future (भर् + इष्य + आमि). ‘I shall bear, sustain’ — the verb from which the name Śākambharī (11.49) is made.
आ (आङ्) with the ablative marks a limit: आ वृष्टेः ‘until the rain’. The text writes it joined (आवृष्टेः); it is not a compound, since वृष्टेः keeps its own case ending.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) सुराः, ततः अहम् आ वृष्टेः आत्मदेहसमुद्भवैः प्राणधारकैः शाकैः अखिलं लोकं भरिष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject अहम्, verb भरिष्यामि, object अखिलं लोकम्; the instrument शाकैः with two epithets; आ वृष्टेः gives the limit of time.
mantras.lit: Then I, O gods, shall sustain the whole world, until the rain, with life-sustaining vegetables arisen from my own body.
mantras.tr: Then, O gods, until the rains return, I shall feed the whole world with life-giving plants grown from my own body.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Until the rains return’ renders आ वृष्टेः, ‘until the rain’; ‘feed’ renders भरिष्यामि, ‘sustain, nourish’.

comm.t: In the drought the Goddess feeds the world from her own body: edible plants that keep life going until the rain comes. The verse prepares her name in 11.49, Śākambharī, ‘she who bears (the world with) vegetables’.

The image of the Goddess as the one who feeds is old in Śākta devotion: Śākambharī is worshipped as the giver of food in famine. The verse itself is precise about the limit — आ वृष्टेः, only until the rain — the Goddess sustains, and the ordinary order resumes.

flags.uncertain: The printed आवृष्टेः is divided here as आ + वृष्टेः (‘until the rain’), the reading of the usual translations. Taking आवृष्टि as one noun (‘rainfall’, ablative ‘from the rain’) makes poorer sense of the verse.

a + ā → ā; the final m is anusvāra before the m of महासुरम् (8.3.23).

samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (√भृ with the suffix khac, which inserts m after the first member; feminine in -ī)
samasa.sense: she who sustains the world with plants (11.48)
the asura called Durgama, ‘hard to approach’

morph.note: Pāṇini’s grammar uses वध as a replacement of √हन् only in the aorist and the benedictive; a future वधिष्यामि is not classical but is common in epic and Purāṇic Sanskrit (ārṣa). It recurs in 11.53.
Future of √या (aniṭ: या + स्य + आमि). With विख्यातिम्, ‘I shall go to fame’, i.e. become famous.

mantras.anvaya: तदा अहं भुवि शाकम्भरी इति विख्यातिं यास्यामि। तत्र एव च दुर्गमाख्यं महासुरं वधिष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: (1) अहं … विख्यातिं यास्यामि with the name in an इति phrase; (2) तत्र एव च … वधिष्यामि with its object.
mantras.lit: Then I shall go to renown on earth as ‘Śākambharī’; and right there I shall slay the great asura named Durgama.
mantras.tr: Then I shall be famed on earth as Śākambharī, and in that same descent I shall slay the great asura called Durgama.
mantras.tr_note: ‘In that same descent’ interprets तत्र एव, ‘right there’.

comm.t: The second name of the third descent: Śākambharī, ‘she who sustains with plants’, from the deed of 11.48. In the same appearance (तत्र एव) she slays a great asura named Durgama, whose name gives her third name in 11.50.

The text says nothing more of Durgama. Later Śākta retellings, such as the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa, make him the cause of the drought: having taken the Vedas from the gods by a boon, he stopped the sacrifices, and the rains failed. The Devī Māhātmya gives only the name and the slaying.
